prompt.context: Six months out of HBS, a frustrated classmate calls you to complain that the fast food burger joint that he bought has been steadily losing money for the last 3 months.
prompt.question: He wants to know what you think he should do about it. Where do you start?

clarifying_info.q: What do you mean by 'losing money'? Have profits declined or is the business in the red?
Have revenues decreased, costs increased, or both?
Are there fewer paying customers, or are customers spending less per visit?
clarifying_info.a: In this case, there are fewer customers (though both could play a role).

clarifying_info.q: Is the issue primarily internal or external?
clarifying_info.a: The issue is external and is driven by a new competitor that opened across the street.

clarifying_info.q: What is the new competitor's value proposition? Are they offering different food, better quality, or lower prices?
clarifying_info.a: They serve chicken dinners and appear to offer a completely different experience.

framework: Diagnose the profit decline: revenues down vs. costs up (or both)
If revenues down: fewer customers vs. lower spend per customer
If fewer customers: external factors (new competition, demographic/economic change, area business closures) vs. internal factors (food quality, pricing, health incident, operations)
Identify the root cause and prioritize drivers by impact
Develop and evaluate options to address root cause
Recommend action plan with timing and responsibilities

questions.prompt: What initial questions should the candidate ask to frame the analysis?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies both revenue and cost dimensions first, then drills into customer count vs. ticket size, and raises both external factors (competition, local economic changes) and internal factors (quality, pricing, health incidents). The candidate should demonstrate a structured, MECE approach and cross off hypotheses as they are ruled out.

questions.prompt: The new competitor serves chicken dinners and seems to offer a different experience. How would you get a deeper understanding of their value proposition?
questions.guidance: A strong answer has three phases: (1) First-hand observation — visit both locations and assess food quality, pricing, variety/healthier options, service, cleanliness, facility layout, parking, and access. (2) Primary customer research — conduct interviews at both locations; pay customers to rate both and determine overlap (former burger customers now exclusive chicken customers, customers who visit both, and brand-new chicken customers who would never visit the burger joint). (3) Data-driven options analysis — synthesize findings into improvement areas (new menu options, facility upgrades, taste/quality), evaluate each on speed-to-traffic-recovery and ROI, prioritize, and develop an action plan with timing and responsibilities.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors could explain why there are fewer customers at the burger restaurant?

categories.name: External — Competition
ideas: New competitor opened nearby offering a different product (chicken dinners)
Competitor offers better perceived value, variety, or experience

categories.name: External — Market/Economic
ideas: Change in local eating habits or dietary preferences
Major employer or business closed in the area reducing foot traffic
Broader economic downturn reducing discretionary spending

categories.name: Internal — Product
ideas: Decline in food quality or consistency
Menu lacks variety or healthier options

categories.name: Internal — Operations/Brand
ideas: Decline in service quality or speed
Health code violation or food safety incident
Crime or safety perception issues around the location

recommendation: Conduct first-hand competitive assessment of the new chicken restaurant and the burger joint across food quality, pricing, variety, service, and facility
Run primary customer research (interviews, intercepts) at both locations to quantify customer overlap and identify the key drivers of switching
Prioritize improvement initiatives by expected traffic recovery speed and ROI; likely candidates include menu expansion, facility refresh, and targeted promotions to win back lost customers
risks: The burger format may face a structural disadvantage against a differentiated chicken competitor that cannot be overcome without significant capital investment
Customer perception damage (if linked to a negative event) may require a longer recovery timeline
Improvement initiatives may not yield sufficient traffic recovery to return the business to profitability
next_steps: Complete competitive mystery-shop and customer interviews within 2-4 weeks
Model financial impact of top 3 improvement scenarios
Decide whether to invest in a turnaround or evaluate exit/sale options if the unit economics cannot be restored
